subsubtopic: SUGGESTED STUDY OF SOCIAL CREDIT MONETARY SYSTEM TO COMBAT INFLATION-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to the terms of Standing Order 43, I request unanimous consent of the House to present a motion dealing with an important and urgent matter.
As the anti-inflation measures of the government are running into vigorous opposition on the part of workers, who are proving thereby that they have no confidence in the proposals of the government, and as the confidence of the people is an essential condition of the success of any measure intended to contain and check inflation, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Beaudoin):
That the House study, as soon as possible, the monetary measures suggested by hon. members of the Social Credit Party of Canada with a view to putting an end to the ravages of inflation through the implementation of an annual guaranteed income paid to all, and the application of a retail discount to the purchase of all essential goods.

subsubtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM-ATTITUDE OF PROVINCES TOWARDS CONTROLLING PROFESSIONAL INCOMES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. In view of the concern of many people that under the government's wage, income and price control program, professional incomes are not likely to be effectively controlled, did the government put forward specific proposals before the provincial finance ministers yesterday in this area? Also, can he inform the House whether some form of agreement was reached by which professional incomes will be brought within the controls program?
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
subsubtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM-ATTITUDE OF PROVINCES TOWARDS CONTROLLING PROFESSIONAL INCOMES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the meeting had before it the proposal in the white paper with regard to the control of professional income. I can say that there was general agreement with the concept that the pricing of professional services should be controlled with the co-operation of the provinces through the control of billing practices by each of the professions. In that sense, there was general agreement in that regard.
With respect to the incomes of professionals as opposed to the pricing of their services, there was not an agreement among the provinces. Some favoured a surtax, either on the whole or over a certain level of an individual's income. Some favoured none at all. There was a spectrum of opinion among the provinces but a conclusion to the effect that the federal government would have to make the final determination on any action that might be taken against incomes above and beyond that provided for by the guidelines.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM-REASON FOR REJECTION BY FEDERAL GOVERNMENT OF SURTAX ON PROFESSIONAL INCOMES

No final determination has been made by the government on the question of surtax. One of the purposes of putting that issue before the meeting was to get a definitive reading from ministers of their positions. As I say, opinion was almost equally divided among three different positions.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, decisions of far reaching importance for the future of the Canadian Armed Forces have been made by the government, and I wish at this time to inform the House of the conclusions the government has reached at this stage of the defence structure review.
The government has confirmed the four priority roles of the Department of National Defence, which are: first of all, a commitment to the defence, security and sovereignty of Canada; secondly, a commitment to the defence of North America; thirdly, a commitment to collective security within the NATO alliance; and fourthly, a commitment to

our country's unique and important contribution to international peacekeeping.
The conclusions of the defence structure review confirm that Canada will continue to have a combined regular and reserve force of more than 100,000 personnel, made up of
78,000	regular personnel and 22,000 reserve personnel. This combined regular and reserve force of 100,000 will ensure that the Canadian Armed Forces will continue to be able to protect Canadian sovereignty, to contribute to national security, and to provide the timely reaction to any civil emergency tasks to which only the forces can respond.
The government recognizes that substantial modernization and replacement of major items of military equipment must be started immediately in order to ensure that the Canadian Armed Forces maintain their capability to carry out effectively their four priority roles.
Other major decisions that I wish to announce are: first, Canada will continue to maintain in Europe a land force and an air force designed and equipped to contribute a strong combat capability to NATO's collective defence of the central region. Second, modern and effective main battle tanks will be provided, either by retrofit or acquisition of new tanks, in order to ensure that our army contingent in Europe possesses the necessary up to date equipment to fulfil its assigned tasks beside our NATO partners. Negotiations for the acquisition of new tanks, or the complete modernization of our present tank force, are to be initiated immediately.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DEFENCE STRUCTURE REVIEW

Other related costs, including spare parts, ground data centres, federal sales tax, contingencies and an allowance for inflation between now and final delivery, will bring the total expenditure to approximately $950 million. The new aircraft will be designed primarily to carry out military tasks essential to North America and NATO defence, as well as providing us with a much improved capability to carry out the long-range surveillance needed to protect our growing sovereignty interests in the waters off our coasts and in the Arctic.

Particularly significant to the future of national defence is the fact that the government has recognized the need to compensate for inflation in the department's personnel, operations and maintenance budgets for next year and in subsequent years.
To conform with the government's policy of economic restraint, the Department of National Defence will find from within its currently planned budget the funds required next year for the start of the tank and the long-range patrol aircraft programs. In following years, the government has agreed that capital expenditures for defence are to be increased, in real terms, by 12 per cent each year for the next five years until capital expenditures reach at least 20 per cent of the total defence budget.
As part of the defence structure review, there has been an assessment of the infrastructure required to support the operational components of the forces. Infrastructure includes headquarters, bases, training and educational facilities and logistics. In aggregate, this infrastructure support requires a large part of the total personnel and financial commitment of the defence program. Over the years there has been some consolidation in these areas, but I believe that our present infrastructure is still larger than is needed to support our operational forces, and for that reason some further consolidation of these support facilities could achieve cost savings without impairing our operational capability. For that reason, I intend to make recommendations to cabinet within the next few months concerning a better balance of support capability to operational capability, which will increase proportionately our combat capability relative to our infrastructure and support facilities.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, hon. members will agree that these decisions are of far reaching significance for the Canadian Armed Forces and for Canada and, in fact, for the NATO alliance. Our national commitment to the protection of Canadian sovereignty and to the preservation of freedom has been reinforced once again by the decisions taken by the Canadian government. There is every reason to believe that these decisions will boost the morale of the Canadian Armed Forces and will increase still further the pride which Canadians have in the dedicated and capable men and women who serve Canada in our armed forces.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the minister for providing me with an advance copy of his statement. First may I say that we in
National Defence
this party welcome this belated indication showing that the government may finally have turned a corner in their treatment of Canada's forces. The scales seem finally to have dropped from the Prime Minister's eyes.
It is interesting to note the timing of the announcement. Last spring the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), went to Europe seeking his personal Holy Grail, a contractual link with western Europe. It is common knowledge that our European allies, particularly West Germany, were refreshingly blunt: the contractual link was to be tied with a NATO knot. It will be one of the delicious ironies of history that the Canadian forces are indebted as much to the German Chancellor for their equipment as to their own government. An assist goes to the Secretary General of NATO, Mr. Luns, who found the situation so serious that he broke all the rules of protocol for his position by speaking out in public about Canada's inadequacy in equipment.
As for the equipment, one's immediate reaction to the selection of the Lockheed aircraft with an American avionics package is to ask, whatever became of the Canadian input into the electronics business? The minister's flatulent press release of December, 1973, said in part:
The contract definition phase will include the employment opportunities and industrial benefits which will accrue to Canada.
Then further:
Proposals from all four contractors indicated a substantial involvement by Canadian companies in the construction of the proposed LRPA, as well as the manufacture of the necessary electronic and surveillance systems.
The question is, will the commitment made by the minister be carried out; will Canadian firms receive some of these contracts? The government seems confused about its defence needs, still not having made up its mind whether to buy new tanks or to refit older ones. I hope the government will seriously consider the Leopard II, which is a superior tank. Also, we should consider the question of a retrofitted, 30-year old Centurion tank which, according to CDS, will cost $750,000 to refit. I believe that new tanks can be purchased for about the same cost. I hope the minister will provide a firmer answer as soon as possible with regard to the tanks.
The minister's message obviously misses two large and important aspects of defence. Firstly, there is no mention of future shipbuilding for our navy, which will likely be requiring patrol vessels in the foreseeable future. Given the length of time required between the decision to build, and delivery-some six years-now is the time for decision if we are to be in any way prepared to patrol a 200-mile fishing or commercial zone.
Finally, the minister's remarks say little about the changing mode of warfare. Now is the time when we should be hearing the minister's thoughts on cruise missiles. Are we considering airborne warning and control systems? On page 4 of the minister's statement he said: "In following years, the government has agreed that capital expenditures for defence are to be increased, in real terms, by 12 per cent each year". With military inflation running at 28 per cent to 30 per cent, I do not know how we can possibly keep our head above water and find the money to

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister based his statement on the defence program upon four major priorities: the defence of Canadian sovereignty, the defence of the North American continent, support of the NATO alliance, and assisting in peacekeeping operations around the world. It is almost impossible to deal with these bits and pieces of announcements by the Department of National Defence without recognizing that all of them have been based on a major fallacy. We are not a great military power. Since the end of World War II we have been trying to ape the great military powers, with the result that we do a little bit of everything but do not do anything particularly well.
A country of 23 million people has to recognize that it must set one or two priorities for things it can do properly, without trying to do other things which are beyond its financial capacity. There can be no doubt about the top priority: there must be greater emphasis and greater expenditure of money-whatever it may require-for the defence of our sovereignty and for the patrolling of our coastal waters and our northern areas, so that Canada may let the world know it is in a position not only to defend itself but to see that its waters and air space are not violated.
I think that North American defence is the number two priority, although I would not necessarily want to see it carried on in the form it is at present. I doubt that NORAD has given us value for the amount of money we have been investing in it, nor do I think we should be tied up in a North American air defence program to the extent that we are today.
I would place the third priority on Canada's peacekeeping role on which we spend a relatively small amount of money compared to our total expenditure. This is the kind of contribution which Canada is uniquely fitted to make. The great superpowers, and even many of the major powers, because of their imperialist background and their days of colonial possessions are not acceptable in regard to supplying peacekeeping forces in some areas of the world. This is a service for which Canada is particularly suited and able to fill, because Canadians generally are recognized as not having any territorial ambitions. Our troops have been well disciplined and well accepted wherever they have been used. This is the kind of role which Canada can play in an increasing measure.
I would put at the bottom of the priorities the support of the NATO alliance. First, this is going to be a very expensive role for us to fill. Already, as the minister has indicated, something must be done about the battle tanks which we have in our NATO forces in Europe. Apparently the government has not made up its mind, but it will have to decide whether to refit the Centurion tanks, which I understand can be done for about 50 per cent of the cost of buying new tanks but will have only half the life expectancy. What their comparison is in fire-power, I do not know. I hope the minister will tell us in the question period. However, this is a decision which will have to be made.

Whether the Centurions are refitted, or new tanks are purchased, it will mean a veby large capital investment. If we are going to keep troops in Europe, they ought to be equipped with the very best military equipment that can be procured. However, such an expenditure, on top of the expenditure for new interceptors which will have to be purchased if we are going to keep forces in Europe, will place a very heavy burden upon the Canadian defence budget.
The time has come when we ought to be phasing out our NATO responsibilities. I know the government made a move to reduce the number of troops. When we entered into the NATO alliance surely we did not commit ourselves to staying in Europe forever. I know that snide remarks have been made by some European statesmen. The suggestion has been made that if we do not put more troops and capital equipment into NATO, we may have some difficulty realizing the fond hope of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), namely, a contractual link in Europe. I hope the government is not going to be intimidated by a suggestion like that. The Republic of France, which is a member of the European Economic Community, has withdrawn its military forces from the control of NATO. No one has suggested they should get out of the European Economic Committee or even the NATO Alliance. I doubt very much whether the four roles outlined by the minister can be fulfilled within the financial capability of the people of Canada. If we are to carry out the other roles effectively and efficiently, the NATO role will have to be substantially and steadily reduced.
The main announcement made by the minister was the fact that the government proposes to purchase, at a cost of $950 million, the Lockheed P3 long-range patrol aircraft, which I understand is the Orion with some modifications. This plane has been used by the United States navy and, I understand, has proven to be very serviceable.
There can be no argument as to the need at this time for an effective, new, long-range aircraft and there can be no argument about the fact that the Argus has now outlived its usefulness. Whether or not the Lockheed Orion is the best plane to replace the Argus, I for one-and I am sure this applies to most of my colleagues in the chamber-am not competent to judge. I think we must leave that to the minister, in consultation with his advisers.
The question I wish to raise is, what part of the $950 million for the Lockheed is to be spent in Canada to provide jobs for Canadians and to put some muscle into the Canadian aircraft industry? Ministers have been singularly evasive when answering questions about the Canadian aircraft industry. The situation is that the government has already acquired de Havilland and has an option to purchase Canadair. I understand the option expires in December, but it is quite possible it might be extended. I am informed that MacDonnell-Douglas have suggested that if de Havilland and Canadair could be merged, they would be prepared to take a small equity position in the new organization. If the F-15 were to be purchased by the Department of National Defence, they would be prepared to put 20 per cent of the total cost of the package into contracts with the merged corporation of Canadair and de Havilland. I do not know whether the
November 27, 1975

press reports are accurate in this respect. As I say, we have been unable to get any direct information from the government. I asked the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Jamieson) some questions about this the other day. He was most evasive, to say the least, though, of course, in a most pleasant way.
We ought to know these things. Is there a package arrangement by which a certain proportion of this $950 million will be spent in Canada or does the government intend to allow the Canadian aircraft industry to go down the drain? What will the government do with Canadair? Is there a role for Canadair either in the building of long-range planes or reconnaissance planes in the future?
Other matters beside the question of national defence are at stake here. There is the question whether or not this large sum of money which parliament is being asked to vote is to be used to help develop an aircraft industry in Canada and provide jobs for Canadians. If we fail to take such a course, we shall become increasingly dependent upon United States or other foreign manufacturers of aircraft for our supplies.
To me, it is inconceivable that in this modern age, a highly industrialized nation like Canada should allow its small aircraft industry to wither away. I hope that when the minister is answering questions, this is one of the questions he will deal with so we may know what the government intends to do about de Havilland and Canadair, and whether these firms, either separately or together, will have anything to expect from this sum of nearly a billion dollars which the government is spending on long-range aircraft.

I am sure the minister is familiar with the condition of these old tanks. I saw them three years ago when, as military critic, I inspected the base there. subsubtopic: ASSURED MAIL SERVICE IN DELTA
speechtext: With reference to the answer to Question No. 234 which stated that assured mail service would be going into Delta by the spring of 1975, has such a programme been instituted and, if not, on what date is the latest expectation on the starting of such service?

speakeroldname: Mr. Paul E. McRae (Parliamentary Secretary to Postmaster General):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General
subsubtopic: ASSURED MAIL SERVICE IN DELTA
speechtext:
While it was our intention to extend the assured mail programme to Delta, our detailed study of the situation there revealed that the application of the normal criteria for assured mail would not improve service to customers of the Delta Post Office and it would increase costs. For example, should a morning collection be made the volume would be small and, with the exception of mail for Delta itself, would have to be sent to Vancouver for inclusion with mail originating there. This additional handling would tend to negate the advantage gained by earlier collection. On the other hand, by maintaining the later collection time presently in effect, sufficient volume is mailed to make up direct bags to several centres in western
Order Paper Questions
Canada and the service accorded these mails is the best that can be achieved considering all the factors. At the same time it is possible to provide next day delivery for mails destined to Vancouver, Victoria, New Westminster, Surrey and White Rock. Considering all the factors we have concluded that extension of the assured mail programme to Delta would not result in any appreciable improvement in service, consequently we have cancelled our plans for extending the programme at this time. You can be assured, however, that our officers in the Delta area will maintain a continuing review of the situation and introduce changes which will benefit the customers of the Delta Post Office.

speechtext: The House resumed, from Tuesday, November 25, consideration of Bill C-73, to provide for the restraint of profit margins, prices, dividends and compensation in Canada, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs; and motion No. 6 (Mr. Macdonald (Rosedale)).

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it will be recalled that the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) raised a question about the recommendation which preceded this bill, in that he found some difference between the bill and the recommendation upon which it was founded. As I recall, sir, you indicated that to some extent at least you shared his views. I have now obtained a revised recommendation from His Excellency the Governor General for Bill C-73.
There has been discussion among representatives of the parties and I understand there would be agreement to the procedure that this revised recommendation should be substituted for the original recommendation and printed in today's Votes and Proceedings.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext: Order, please. The proposal put by the hon. President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp) has been heard. There is an indication that there may be agreement to it. Is that the case?

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Generally there is agreement, Mr. Speaker, although I still have some very grave complaints as to the form as a whole. Without wanting to begin taking it apart, and I am not going to insist upon any change at this time which might block our progress and require a ruling, there is one last point that does concern me. With all due respect to the government House leader, I do not think the final phrase "or as provided in the said measure" covers the difficulty I raised in respect of section 26(2).
Mr. Speaker was to look at this matter to determine whether the change proposed by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) had met my original objection, in respect of which His Honour had indicated some agreement. On a contingency basis there could be grave difficulty. However, in order to set aside, or to put at rest this unhappy interlude regarding these recommendations, I am quite prepared to say, on behalf of this party, that this is all right for now, but we surely must have some discussions and arrive at a much better formula for the resolution stage of a bill.
I might also say that I, personally, have some hesitation about the present practice of obtaining revised recommendations. It has become a purely clerical function, and it seems to me these recommendations should have a little more authenticity than that.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think an accommodation has been reached in so far as this piece of legislation is concerned, but I should also like to

support the suggestion of the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), that there might be further discussions about the form of Governor General's recommendations. At this point the hori. member for Edmonton West and I may part. I gather he would like to have the recommendation couched in language that is full of all the details in the bill. I would like to see it go the other way. Maybe that is because I remember the days decades ago when cabinet ministers would stand over there and say, "His Excellency the Governor General, having been made aware of the subject matter of this bill, is pleased to approve the same and recommends it to the consideration of the House."
I wonder what value there is to an exercise of having some clerical operation produce a long Governor General's recommendation which is changed every time we change the bill. I think a little reading of the history of this device going back 300 or 400 years to how money bills came from the Crown, and so on, would produce the solution I suggest, namely, a much shorter and more generalized recommendation.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Order, please. The discussions, of course, about the relationship between the recommendation and the bill and subsequent powers or restrictions to amending powers is a most interesting one. Indeed, frankly it is not altogether clear in the relationship between the recommendation and the bill. There is, of course, the countervailing difficulty that the more general the recommendation becomes, the more it is possible to argue that it then becomes applicable to every provision of the bill and not just to the financial provisions of the bill, and therefore every amendment would have to carry in it the direct recommendation. In any case, it is an interesting discussion which could carry us away, I am sure, all afternoon, and this is not the desire of hon. members.
It appears at the moment that an accommodation has been reached. The amended recommendation, if I understand it correctly without reading it in every detail, is the same as it was except for the addition of the wording at the end, "or as provided in the said measure", which relates to the expiry date of the bill. That would seem to me, at first reading in any case, to cover the specific instances that have already been argued and discussed and to which the House has already directed its attention. Is there unanimous consent to receive the recommendation?

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext: Agreed.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION

Mr. Speaker, now that you can hear me, I hope, I should like to say that I and my colleagues have taken the position that this legislation is still totally inadequate for the protection of farm income in respect of the production of grain. We feel the legislation is inadequate and its effect is uncertain, particularly the provision which automatically includes all grain producers and the one which allows them to opt out once and come back in, but then to remain in. The purpose of these two amendments is to allow grain producers to opt out of the program at any time and for any number of times. It will allow them to opt out and to opt back in again at their choosing.
This is an unusual amendment to be coming from a member of a socialist party which stands for universal programs in order to maximize the benefits of those programs. They might be called free enterprise amendments, but that is not why I am proud of them. I am convinced this program would prove to be inadequate. Even if it turns out that I am wrong, because of the many uncertainties it would seem to me that for at least the first few years of the program grain producers should have maximum flexibility, being able to opt in and opt out any number of times.
I suspect that the minister will say that this would create a great many administrative difficulties. However, if this grain stabilization measure is as good as the minister thinks and says it is, then I imagine he would have very little fear of any significant number of farmers frequently opting in and out of the program. If the program is going to be as good as he claims, then I do not understand why he should worry about accepting these amendments.
I hope my friends in the official opposition will take the position that because of the uncertainties and inadequacies of the bill, this kind of freedom and flexibility should be available to every grain producer. The minister claims this program is good. I disagree with him. But if he is right, he should have no qualms about accepting these amendments.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin). We discussed this matter at great length in committee and I agree with the hon. member when he suggests this legislation is inadequate and is not what the farmers want. We spent a week travelling throughout the prairie provinces, receiving briefs from farm organizations, wheat pools, farmers' unions, the Pal-liser Grain Growers and others. All the indications were
November 27, 1975

that they were not happy with the bill and, because of its complexities, could not understand it.
As a matter of fact, because of the complexities of the legislation a number of those who presented briefs did not have the opportunity of discussing the measure in detail. Almost without exception, these organizations and individuals indicated that if the legislation worked on an individual pay-out basis, rather than on the basis of a five-year average with a pay-out to the whole Wheat Board area, it might be satisfactory. I hope to have an opportunity of discussing that matter in greater detail at third reading.
In considering the amendments of the hon. member, it would seem at first blush that the individual producers should have the opportunity of opting in and out of the plan as and when they wish. If we consider this opting in and out on the basis suggested by the hon. member we can visualize a difficult situation. When there is a substantial deficit in the fund, the government is required to lend money in order to make a pay-out. If we adopted such a flexible provision, we could have a situation in which farmers, in the initial years of the plan's operation, could obtain substantial pay-outs and then opt out of the plan in good crop years.
We must remember that the fund provides for a $2 to $1 ratio. It would be fairly simple for a producer to remain in the plan for two years, for example, and receive a substantial payment. During this time the fund might get into a deficit position and would have to be replenished by the government. The interest on that money would continue to build up. A producer might be able to obtain four, five or six times the amount he had paid in and then opt out of the plan for a considerable time during good crop years. He might do this knowing that he would have to put money into the plan to help pay off the indebtedness incurred by loans from the federal government, and the interest. Under the circumstances if he were a smart businessman-and I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that the farmers of the prairie provinces are vey smart and shrewd businessmen-I am certain he would opt out and say, "That is it, fellows".
Under the conditions of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre he could opt out of the plan for a long enough period that the indebtedness to the government would be paid off, and then he would simply opt into the plan and take advantage of it. So under these circumstances, personally I cannot support the amendment of the hon. member.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 13,1 was speaking on the motion for the production of papers presented by the hon. member for Vegreville, and in particular the correspondence and agreements between Sunset Crest Ltd. and any employee of Air Canada or its subsidiaries. I had not quite finished my remarks and would like to continue.
I had pointed out, among other things, that Air Canada is a large corporation which, over the years, has been a credit to Canada, and for over 20 years has required no subsidies from the public purse. The company is not asking the government for a penny of financial assistance, quite unlike larger national airlines of some other countries. Its deficit last year was very much smaller than many of its competitors, and the government has not been asked to pay this loss. In 1975, a year of falling traffic due to general economic depression and rising costs due to fuel prices, et cetera, the employees of the company are, I believe, trying to achieve a break even position for the company, against great odds. I do not know whether their objective will be achieved, but I am satisfied that they are cutting costs and developing sales with a view to improving the financial position of the company.
There are staff problems in all companies, private and public, in Canada and other parts of the world. These are solved by the companies' management as they arise, and Air Canada cannot be expected to act differently. There are resignations, dismissals and disciplinary actions in all companies, including Air Canada, and to single out Air Canada for ridicule when these things happen at any level-blue collar, management or executive-is unfair to all those dedicated and hardworking employees who have built their airline to a level of prosperity and service to the nation of which all Canadians can well be proud.
Whatever may come out of the Air Canada inquiry on financial controls and other areas of concern, I want to make one point crystal clear, and that is that the great majority of the employees of Air Canada at all levels- management, executive and other classes-are operating an airline with efficiency, integrity and loyalty and have thereby developed Air Canada to a point where it can earn its place as one of the great airlines of the world, with an operating efficiency which has proved to be comparable with the better run airlines of any nation.
The government has come to realize that the characteristics of the airline business have changed significantly since 1937 when the present Air Canada Act was first brought before this House, and that Air Canada has grown to a level which requires some changes in the present Air Canada Act. I think the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) will be presenting to this House for consideration his proposals to permit Air Canada more flexibility to deal with new business trends, and allow the company to compete more effectively, especially in the international airline market.

November 27, 1975

Hon. members should be provided with ample opportunity to discuss in some detail the matters involving Air Canada, including ventures such as the Sunset Crest Limited transaction, both when the Minister of Transport puts forward his proposal for amendment to the Air Canada Act and when the Air Canada inquiry report is presented to the House.
I should again like to stress a point I made when taking part in a similar debate on a motion for production of papers earlier in the session. That point is that all hon. members would like to see as much information made available as could be made available. In this regard we on this side of the House are faced with the same limitation as those across the way, and as our duties and obligations to those we represent are similar, we share the same frustration when unable to obtain a certain document or piece of information which we may deem pertinent in carrying out these duties.
During this session I have had the opportunity of serving on the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments. This experience has left me with an appreciation of both the importance and the complexity of the issue of accessibility to government information.
While I am sympathetic to the objective of greater accessibility to information and less secrecy in government, at the same time I recognize that free and unlimited access to all information and documents is impossible, or certainly unwise. Similarly, I find the guidelines which indicate several categories of restrictions for the production of government papers and documents too general and far reaching, but at the same time I concede that their introduction was a very considerable step forward in that they underline the acceptance of the principle that the government has to justify its withholding of facts, and they also provide a focus for constructive criticism and suggestions for a greater flow of information.
I thank the hon. member for presenting his motion, which provided an opportunity to discuss the subject of availability of government information in general, and in particular information pertaining to Air Canada transactions. However, I am unable to agree with his motion.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege for me to take part in this debate on production of papers and to follow the hon. member for Toronto-Lake-shore (Mr. Robinson). I can assure the hon. member that my view is quite polarized from his, and I hope that my contribution in this debate will change his mind. Unlike his, it is my belief that Air Canada can be expected to act differently. It has to act differently as a national airline if we are to set conditions, a pace, and a standard of behaviour for other corporate activities in Canada.
I remind this House that this Crown corporation, Air Canada, and its subsidiaries have advantages which are a businessman's dream. Air Canada has the highest occupancy rate in the airline business, which is literally a licence to print money in that industry. It has a monopoly position with its choice of routes, and it has access to all government boards and agencies. It has unlimited money available at the government's cost of money, and the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore in his address in this
Air Canada
debate last November 13 proudly pointed out that it has not been necessary for over two decades for public money to subsidize Air Canada. However, that money is available and has been available pretty well on an unlimited basis at a cost of money available to no other organization in Canada.
Air Canada has an insider track on other government agencies' activities which allows it to eliminate or control its Canadian and offshore competition.
However, to be completely fair, one must acknowledge that Air Canada also faces certain disadvantages. It has inherited the disease of its present owner in that for each $100 of revenue the CNR has to spend between $100 and $101 to earn it, whereas its major competitor, which has an incentive factor built in and which has to answer to taxpaying shareholders, spends $90 to earn $100 of revenue.
This apathy for want of an incentive and a need to be accountable to taxpaying shareholders has obviously spilled over into Air Canada attitudes and management. Air Canada does not pay its taxes; it only accrues them. It currently owes an amount in excess of $29 million, which is down from the $34 million it owed, according to last year's estimate, as a result of last year's loss.
Air Canada does not pay the interest due on the moneys which have been lent to it by the government. It accrues this interest, and has accrued some $55 million in interest. It does not return or retire its borrowings, as normal corporations have to do in a free enterprise economy. Along with these unfortunate business practices, it is overstaffed with 25 per cent too many people.
The situation in Air Canada is now an acknowledged disgrace, and if the government will allow the opposition to assist in cleaning out the rot and questionable practices which exist within its corporate structure, perhaps we can then get our national airline flying with the measure of pride its employees and the people of Canada once held for it.

This is hard earned respect; they have worked for it. It has come to them through good training facilities and good personnel discipline. I am proud of those of my constituents who work for Air Canada, and I am proud of Air Canada.
I want to take issue with a previous speaker who, when talking about the airline business in Canada, made comparisons between Air Canada and some private carriers. Perhaps he forgets that when Air Canada was formed in the thirties, the original purpose of the company was to establish a basic air service across Canada even where there was not a substantial amount of profit. It was not just designed to serve the lucrative routes. I suggest that those private airlines that are doing so well would have to spread their services thinly if they were asked to compete on all the routes that Air Canada serves. This is not to say that there are not perhaps problems within Air Canada, or no deep seated concerns expressed by some of their own employees. The report that will be tabled in the House in the near future will bring some of those problems to light. I hope the government will move quickly to deal with them, and I am confident that it will.
I have toured many of Air Canada's facilities for training pilots, and maintenance facilities across Canada. I
Air Canada
doubt that any airline in the country has a better operating record.
The financial aspect has been mentioned. I understand that Mr. Estey's report will deal with that. That inquiry was set up primarily to look into that area.
From my reading of Canada's airline industry I would say that Air Canada has gone through the generation change of aircraft perhaps better than many other airlines. Some United States airlines are mothballing planes, or selling planes at fire sale prices just to get them off their books. Even though Air Canada has incurred a loss during the last year the company still compares well with the United States airlines.
Many of the airlines that hon. members claimed were managed efficiently went over to wide-bodied planes, and then found that they had completely misjudged the market. As a result they had a tremendous over-capacity in their fleets and some nearly went bankrupt. Furthermore, there was a severe cutback in service-a cutback that we would not want Air Canada to introduce in our remote areas-or through mergers where some companies were simply put out of business.
I would ask some members who are critical of Air Canada to remember that many of the routes are not profitable. However, Air Canada provides a service to all parts of the country, and this is not the case with the private carriers. If the performance of Air Canada is compared to many United States airlines, I think Air Canada shows up rather well in terms of competent management.
A few years ago when Air Canada was hiring employees, it was regarded as a privileged occupation. Stewardesses, for instance, had to be graduate nurses and there was great restriction on who could compete for the job vacancies. Today, many more people are flying; perhaps the mystique has decreased and that has not helped the morale problems to which reference has been made.
I do not intend to go on and extol the virtues of Air Canada. I just want to say I have some very close friends and good constituents who work for Air Canada. Those people are proud of Air Canada and do their best to give Canada good air service.

In this whole business of Air Canada, as with other Crown corporations, we have found the government party to the veil of secrecy. There has been far too much secrecy in the analysis of the operations of this Crown corporation, Mr. Speaker. In my view parliamentary committees have become an ineffective mechanism to review the operations of a corporation such as Air Canada. We should be reminded that the last annual report of Air Canada considered by a parliamentary committee was the 1970 annual report. That certainly is not satisfactory.
The last time officials of Air Canada appeared before the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications was in November, 1973. We have seen all these shady deals and questionable actions taking place, but to this point in time we have not had the Air Canada people before a parliamentary committee to justify their actions or answer the allegations that have been levelled against them.
One has to be shocked at the government's continuing efforts to cover up information which parliament deserves, and which the public rightly deserves. -the government has an obligation to provide full, objective and timely information; and that the citizens have a right to such information.

speechtext:
We are, as soon as I and several others get through persuading the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) of the justice of this amendment. The amendment covers items that I have heard the minister himself say are legitimate costs of production for farm producers. If the minister reads the motion I know he will get to his feet and agree that it coincides exactly with his views on proper costs of production for agricultural producers.
The motion adds to the criteria in the bill. The new subparagraphs read:
(i)	depreciation on farm machinery and equipment used for grain production or used in the farm business in respect of grain production and transportation.
(j)	interest charges incurred in respect of the production or sale of grain; and
(k)	producer levies in respect of this Act.
I agree with the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board, and it is very rare that happens, but interest payments on land is not a cost of production because land has appreciated in all years except the dirty thirties. As a rule, land appreciates in value. Interest payments on land are really part of a capital investment which will be recovered, and then some, when the land is sold. However, surely the Minister of Agriculture will agree that interest payments on farm buildings and equipment required for the production of grain is a legitimate cost of production. Those items all depreciate, and depreciate rapidly.
The Government of Canada, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen), and their predecessors, for many years have

allowed interest charges on machinery, buildings and equipment as a legitimate expense. If such an expense is not a cost of production, I have never seen one. This is already allowed in the taxation laws of Canada. Interest on machinery, equipment and buildings is allowed as an expense by several marketing boards. I am sure the Minister of Agriculture will agree that it is a legitimate cost of production. That is why I asked the Minister of Agriculture a couple of questions the other day about marketing boards and the anti-inflation bill.
If the criteria for cost of production that are enclosed in Bill C-41 are applied by the Anti-Inflation Board, farmers in the minister's area and mine will get it in the neck when it comes to restraint. There are farmers in my constituency and in that of the minister's whose payments annually for interest charges on loans for farm machinery, equipment and buildings go anywhere from several hundred dollars to $2,000 to $3,000.
The Professional Association of Accountants, federal income tax laws, several marketing boards, universities, farm management groups, and farm organizations all recognize that this is a legitimate cost of production. Why then does the minister in charge of the wheat board exclude it from this bill?
As I said earlier, I agree that interest payments on land can be excluded, but how can you exclude interest payments on machinery, equipment and buildings? The interest on a frame granary and machine shed is only about 5 per cent a year. That is not a big deal to the government. It is not a big deal to the grain stabilization board; However, it is big to the farmer making the payments.
There is a further point, the matter of depreciation. Again the income tax laws permit depreciation on machinery, equipment and buildings as a legitimate expense of production, a legitimate part of the cost of producing a bushel of grain for the six grains under this bill. That has been the law of the land since World War I. However, the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board says it cannot be allowed under this bill.
I am sure that depreciation is computed as a legitimate part of the cost of production by CEMA. Egg producers who make loans to buy equipment and put up buildings can include depreciation as a part of their production. That is legitimate, regardless of what Mrs. Plumptre might say.
Costs of production computed by the Saskatchewan Hog Marketing Commission include the cost of loans made by farmers to erect small barns and the ancillary equipment needed for them. Depreciation on buildings and equipment is a legitimate expense and legitimate part of the cost of production. However, for grain producers the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board says it is not part of the cost of production formula. Surely the Minister of Agriculture cannot agree with that. I cannot. I know that a number of farmers sitting on the opposite side of the House cannot agree with it. Why cannot we have a cost of production formula which is relatively uniform across the country? Why is there the exception for producers under this so-called grain income stabilization plan?
I wish to say a word now about the stabilization fee, the 2 per cent premium to be paid under the plan. That is the

same as a crop insurance premium, the same as other insurance premiums, sickness and accident insurance premiums, car insurance and truck insurance premiums, all of which farmers are allowed to deduct as an expense under the income tax laws, all of which are included as a legitimate cost of production under CEMA and 20 or 30 other marketing boards across Canada. It is deductible. But in the bill before us it suddenly ceases to be a cost of production.
A farmer who delivers, say, $25,000 worth of grain pays 2 per cent into the fund, that is, $500. That is his premium. If he comes under a marketing board, that is considered part of his cost of production. I have yet to hear any argument from the minister in charge of the Wheat Board, from the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale), or the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley (Mr. Mclsaac) as to why this should not be a legitimate deduction, as it is under the Income Tax Act or under marketing boards for other commodities.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak in favour of this amendment. I will speak in support of it because of the way the payment is triggered. The formula to which the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) referred has been prepared by bureaucrats in the Department of Agriculture and I can only describe it as a statistical wonder. It will keep Statistics Canada hiring people to go around the country and gather all the information required by the formula, one
Grain Stabilization
which comprises sections from (a) to (o). At the moment we are discussing section (b) relating to gross expenses.
As I look at the situation I see interest rates incurred by agriculture increasing dramatically in the years to come. I play with statistics a little myself from time to time, and I have examined the amount of credit outstanding in the agricultural sector today. It was difficult to come up with these figures because Statistics Canada does not collect them. However, various credit agencies gave me figures; I do not claim they are totally accurate but they are the best I could come up with.
The figures show that between 1968-72 long term credit in Canada amounted to some $2,132,000,000, intermediate credit to some $1,808,000,000, and short-term credit to around $1,933,000,000. That is a lot of money. Let us put it in terms we can understand, that is, the average debt per farmer. In 1971 it came to $12,911. It has increased substantially since that time. In 1972 it was $14,433, in 1973 it was $17,295, and in 1974 it was $18,021. That amounts to some $6,000 increase per farmer in the debt carried.
Interest charges have grown heavier not because of the increase of the debt but because interest rates have risen. Interest payments on indebtedness in Canadian agriculture in 1971 amounted to $918 per year per farmer. In a matter of three years this has risen to $1,500. It seems to me that as the cost of land and machinery increases, the loan and interest charges carried by the farmer will rise substantially.
To my mind, in order to make this formula realistic-and if anyone can understand it, statisticians should be able to-it is absolutely necessary that in future years interest charges and depreciation on farm machinery be included in the cost of production formula that will be put into the calculation of the aggregate stabilization payment to determine whether a payment to western farmers is triggered or not triggered. These are the reasons why I feel that this amendment should be supported.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal with the many points raised by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger) and the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin).
The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre suggested that three items should be included in the cost of production formula. To take the last point first, the producer levies, his argument can be disposed of rather quickly by my confirming to him formally that just as producer levies are tax deductible they are also one of the costs included in the calculation of the cost of production in this plan. Clearly under clause 8(3)(f), insurance premiums, such things as producer contributions to a crop insurance plan are included. That is clearly the intention of the legislation, so that particular concern of the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre can be laid to rest rather quickly.
The second point that he mentioned, and which was alluded to by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin in more detail, was the matter of interest. As both hon. members pointed out, long-term interest, which is really investment of money in land or other things, is something that should

November 27, 1975
Grain Stabilization
not be included as a cash cost for operating expenses under the plan because it is something of quite a different nature and would not properly be included in the definition of "cost of production" in this bill.
I think the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre conceded that point; his more basic question had to do with short and medium term interest. Again I suggest to him that that particular matter is covered in the legislation in that the cost of production formula includes the cash costs associated with the production of the grains that are covered by the plan. Any of the items enumerated from paragraph (a) to (h) which involve an expenditure of money at medium or short term interest are therefore included.
If the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre wants to argue the point it may be by implication, but it is very definitely a factor that is included in the survey material that Statistics Canada will be gathering later next spring and the following year. Again medium and long-term interest, where they relate to expenditures for grain production as enumerated in paragraphs (a) to (h), are clearly covered by the bill.
The third point that the hon. member raised in speaking to the amendment is a more complicated one, and I should like to take a few moments to deal with this question of depreciation. As hon. members know, or at least as those who were on our committee in western Canada know, a great many producers raised questions concerning depreciation. There can be no doubt that if you were to ask a producer a very blunt and straightforward question about what he views to be one of this most important cost items, he will probably reply that it is depreciation. It was not very long ago that western Canadian grain producers were literally living off their depreciation. It is an item that is first and foremost on their minds. When one looks at the particular provision in the context of the grain stabilization bill, one can see that the inclusion of depreciation is not something that would enhance the protection that this bill offers western Canadian grain producers.
The first argument that I would offer in support of that is one that may be regarded as economic theory but which is valid in the sense that an expenditure made on machinery or major equipment is not so much a cash expenditure, such as an expenditure on seed, fertilizer, gas or oil- an expenditure that a farmer makes every year in the course of production-but is really a longer term investment. Granted, it is not an investment in a sense of investing in land, which is more or less permanent, but is an investment expenditure.
As I have said, and as other hon. members have indicated, the costs enumerated in this bill are cash costs associated with production in each year. So there is a theoretical difficulty in including an expenditure which, granted, farmers make, but make over the longer term; they do not make it year by year.
The question is: how do you arrive at a fair, reasonable and actuarially sound basis for taking that factor into consideration? A great deal of work has been done in investigating two questions. The first is whether it may legitimately be included in the plan; the second is that, if it is not, what are the methods whereby you can accommodate the suggestion that it should?

The first approach, I suppose, is simply to calculate a standard average figure for depreciation across the board for the prairie region and to plug that figure into the legislation at the appropriate point. The problem there is that it does not change the calculation one bit, because you would add that standard average figure year by year to the moving five year average as well as to the sixth year's specific figure. When you subtract the one figure from the other you end up with exactly the same figure as if you had not added the same factor to both sides. Put simply, five minus three is two, just as four minus two is two. The net result is the same if you add the same figure to both sides and then subtract them one from the other. You have not changed the dollar value at all. Doing this with an across the board average figure would not change the result, and thus you have not improved the protection available to producers under the bill.
The second approach, I suppose, would be to try to come up with the actual figure. Instead of finding an average that you plug in arbitrarily, you come up with the actual figure representing the expenditures made by farmers on major equipment. The difficulty there leads me back to the original theoretical point that I was making about depreciation, and that is that it is an investment expenditure, not so much a cash expenditure year by year.
When you look at the expenditures made by producers over time, they make major expenditures of this kind in their good years. For the purposes of this plan, this would be in the years when the net cash flow is the broadest. They refrain from making major investment expenditures in years when the net cash flow is narrowest. If you were to include the actual figures, you would add the additional or broader expense in the year when the net cash flow is broadest, and therefore the year when you do not need the expense; you would not add it in the year when the net cash flow is narrowest, in the year when the greater expense would justify a payment from the fund.
The real dilemma with this concept is that you add this expense in the wrong years, and you do not add it in the right years, with the net result that the flow of the plan over time is distorted, and the net protection that is available to producers may very well be reduced, not improved, by including depreciation.
For these reasons, both theoretical and practical, I would be opposed to this particular amendment which includes depreciation, which I think takes away from the actuarial soundness of the plan and makes mention of other things such as interest and producer levies which I suggest are already in the bill with the other points enumerated.
I should also like to deal with the argument raised by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin about the alleged great bureaucracy that will be involved in the grain stabilization plan, an army of bureaucrats who will be tramping across the prairies to make the plan effective. I think that is a common allegation, but it is a misconception. The fact of the matter is that it simply is not so.
There will not be a great siege by government employees descending upon the prairies to make this plan work. The Western Grain Stabilization Administration will be located in a rather small office in the city of Winnipeg. I am
November 27, 1975

told the number of permanent employees will be perhaps 12 or 15. During the start-up stages there may be some additional expense involved, but in the longer term I believe the cost of the plan will be something in the order of $300,000.
It is interesting also to look at the cost of the plan in terms of administration compared to the cost of administering provincial crop insurance plans, which some members suggest would be a better plan than this. If you take the cost of the crop insurance plans in the provinces of Saskatchewan, Manitoba or Alberta you will find that this particular plan costs at the very most one-fifth as much as the least expensive of those plans. This plan will not be a burden upon the public treasury. It will not be a burden on the producer in terms of the administrative cost because this cost will not be borne from the fund but entirely by the federal treasury and the Government of Canada. So, in no way can it in fairness be alleged that this plan will create a bureaucratic jungle. Those suggestions simply are not true. I think the proof of the pudding will be in the eating when we see the plan in place, it is to be hoped by January 1, 1976.
I would invite hon. members to think very seriously about the arguments I have put forward particularly in respect of depreciation. I suggest the other points are also included, and I would urge that the amendment be defeated.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I sat in on much of the discussion in the committee. I think one of the great weaknesses in this type of a plan has become apparent tonight.
I have listened over a long period to the minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board indicate that we were talking about stabilization of income, that it was the income that was to be stabilized, and that this would be accomplished through this levy over a period of time. In other words the money would be collected in the good years and the payout would come in the bad years.
The parliamentary secretary tonight changes all that and says that we are operating on an income insurance program rather than income stabilization, that we are using the net cash flow as against net income. He indicates that while it is always made very clear by the minister responsible for the Wheat Board that we are talking about levies and are not talking about insurance, in no way is any percentage of the level of income insured. In other words you do not get poor too fast nor do you get rich too fast.
There is nothing to say you would be insured against becoming poor in a bad year, or that you would be insured against being rich in a good year. If the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale) is confused, so am I. Either he is right or the minister responsible for the bill is right.

I would agree with him if he really had responsibility for this bill. I think we have come a long way forward from that period of three or four years ago when it was totally a stabilization bill and where there was no cost of production included in it. If he is now saying that we are to put in the levies, that this will be part of the cost of production, and that some of the other things like
Grain Stabilization
the interest charges on short-term investment for farm machinery and other short-term investments will be part of the cost of production under this legislation, then I think we have come a long way forward. But I do not think that is in the bill.
I have never seen the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), who is responsible for the wheat board, at any time change his mind. In fact once he makes up his mind, whether he is right or wrong, he never changes it. There is absolutely no flexibility in his mind. I have seen him on occasion lose a bill in this House rather than make any kind of amendment to that bill, no matter how small. He does not change his mind. However, the hon. member for Assiniboia in changing the interpretation of what we are doing really in effect has gone a long way, in my opinion, in making this a much more acceptable bill.
The problem we are having in all sectors of agriculture today is in finding out and spelling out the factors which go into making up the cost of production. We had this difficulty in respect of CEMA. There are the arguments which take place concerning the actual rise in the cost of production which goes into the product. There has been a considerable difference of opinion concerning what constitutes those particular items. In this bill a number of those cost of production items have been delineated.
In addition to that it has been suggested we include such things as the stabilization levy under this bill. If this is called an insurance premium I assume it is covered, but I am not sure what we are talking about in respect of insurance premiums. There are the premiums payable under the provincial insurance programs which also may affect parts of the grain industry that are being covered by this bill. Those are insurance premiums and will be allowed as a cost expense.
The depreciation, in my opinion, was handled very loosely by the hon. member for Assiniboia. He indicated that if income should be high the farmer would spend money on new machinery, and then following a great number of bad years, the farmer would find in another couple of good years that it would be absolutely necessary to replace all the machinery. The farmer would be replacing machinery that had run out of depreciation from an income tax point of view a number of years previously.
* (2120)
Farmers could not buy new machinery because they did not have any money. It was a very simple process. And when they did have some money one of the things they had to do was make an expenditure for modernizing the equipment necessary in their operations.
Hon. members should know that when a farmer runs out of depreciation, it usually indicates there were a number of bad years when he was not able to replace his machinery, no matter how bad it was. He could not replace it, and he could not take advantage of any deduction he might have had with regard to income tax for the simple reason that he had no income. Therefore, he had no depreciation, he could not use any depreciation, and there was also no income tax. There were many years when many farmers found themselves in that position. There are many of us who have been concerned for some time about this problem, and we would like to have the formula established in a way in

November 27, 1975
Grain Stabilization
which it could be applied not only to this piece of legislation but also to the income tax legislation, and to all the other legislation which uses these same criteria or similar criteria in establishing cost of production for a given commodity.
Our legislation has always been pretty sloppy in many ways. I can think of at least five or six different acts where a person is considered to be disabled, and the criteria for establishing disability under the Canada Pension Plan, veterans allowance, workmen's compensation in Ontario, and family benefits legislation are different in each case.
It seems to me that in setting up our cost of production and the items which go into making up cost of production we should be working very hard at getting uniform cost of production criteria which will apply to all legislation farmers may use so that they will not have great difficulty in deciding what is allowed and in which piece of legislation it may be.
The parliamentary secretary continued to talk about net cash flow versus net income, and it seems to me that in this legislation there is no relationship to net cash flow; that that was not the criterion. It also is a fact that this did not start out as a net income insurance program. This was supposed to be a stabilization of farm incomes to take out the highs and lows of fluctuation in farm income. Originally it was not at all concerned with cost of production. Now that it is changed so that the parliamentary secretary can indicate that we are interested in net cash flow, and we must also be interested in what the cost of that production might be.
The amendment before us adds one or two things which the parliamentary secretary is not sure are necessary. He indicates that others are already in the legislation. It seems to me that we are clarifying for the farmer the method of calculating net costs, and if we are able to do that I think we will be providing a service.
Much of this is already embodied in the thinking of the government, and will eventually end up as regulations, so that there should certainly be no objection to passing this amendment proposed by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) because it only amounts to clarification.
If the parliamentary secretary is right, and we are now deciding what the net cash flow will be to provide a net cash income, and that this is an insurance toward that end, then there will not be any difficulty with this amendment as regards the regulations.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was quite interested in the dissertation of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale). He said that some years ago agricultural producers or grain farmers were literally living on depreciation. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, this Liberal government certainly looked after that with its capital gains tax. This is not happening at the present time because of the taxation policy.
He asked how we would arrive at an actuarially sound and equitable base for the figure on cost of production. I do not think you need to be a mathematician to figure that one out, with our present income tax system. It is easy to calculate the actual cost of production on the average grain farm today. All the government would have to do is consider all those parts of the expense that are deductible for tax purposes. That would be equitable and fair, but perhaps it is too simple.
The hon. member for Assiniboia said that depreciation was included in the cost of operations, but I do not see that mentioned anywhere in the bill. In that part of the legislation which refers to the cost of production, everything that is mentioned is something that is purchased. For instance, subclause (3) (b) on page 11 reads:
items purchased by producers to operate and maintain farm machinery used for grain production or used in the farm business in respect of grain production and transportation;
Subparagraph (d) of subclause (3) reads: items purchased by producers to maintain farm buildings used for grain production, but not including items purchased to maintain a home;
Depreciation is not taken into account. It is grossly unfair not to include depreciation as a cost of production, especially as under our tag system we take into account capital gains. Clearly the drafters of this legislation are guilty of omission and gross error. It's a correction that should be given consideration.
We should also consider interest rates. The hon. member for Assiniboia suggested that capital costs for farm machinery are incurred in good years. I agree to some extent, although when the equipment breaks down through no fault of the operator, he must buy new equipment, no matter when it happens. At one time a new tractor would cost several hundred dollars more than the old one, but now, in this day and age of inflation, costs rise by thousands, not hundreds of dollars.
At one time you could buy a fair-sized tractor for $15,000; now it will cost you anywhere from $35,000 to $40,000 or $45,000. Few operators have that kind of cash floating around. This means they must borrow. Goodness only knows, anyone producing anything considers the cost of
