money as sizable input cost. Inevitably the minister will need to consider the question of interest costs.
In addition, we must look at labour costs which rise each consecutive year. Anyone who wants to keep his operation efficient must consider labour costs. As time goes on, more and more producers must hire labour. Agricultural producers must compete with other segments of industry for labour. Therefore costs of labour must be taken into consideration in computing costs of production. I think the minister has overlooked this. Labour costs are increasing rapidly; therefore provision should be included in the bill, along lines suggested by us for protecting the producer.
If I may digress, let me refer hon. members to a discussion which took place in the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs the other day. We were discussing commodity groups and farm marketing boards, a subject of concern to many hon. members as is evident from questions they ask in the House. Hon. members want to know how the Anti-Inflation Board, to be established under Bill C-73, will affect farm marketing boards.
Members of the committee asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) how Bill C-73 would affect the operation of the Canadian Wheat Board. He answered by saying that the minister in charge of the Wheat Board had been involved in the establishment of policy but that, otherwise, he could not answer our questions. Unfortunately the minister in charge of the Wheat Board is not present. Hopefully on third reading he will answer certain questions concerning this bill. It is important legislation, as the Canadian Wheat Board is the largest marketing board in Canada, administering more money than any other board. It is important for us to know how Bill C-73 will affect marketing boards. That question must be answered.
We must also consider payments. What bearing will Bill C-73 have on the $500.00 to be paid in as a premium, deposit,-call it what you will-to the fund? How will payouts be affected by Bill C-73? These questions must be answered before we pass this legislation. I raise this matter because in committee, when we asked the minister if premiums and payments connected with crop insurance would have any effect on the stabilization bill, he said no; then, after being corrected by a member of the department, he made an about face and said yes. Therefore before the bill passes we must hear the answers on certain aspects of the bill which concern Canadian producers.
Many producers are indifferent to this legislation as they plan to retire in five or six years and will not become involved. Nevertheless, our concerns are legitimate and should be answered. On third reading I hope the minister will deal with these matters and, hopefully, answer questions which are of utmost concern to grain producers of western Canada.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE STABILIZATION OF NET PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to participate in the debate on the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Regi-na-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin), but was prompted to speak by the arguments put forward by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale), and the peculiar position taken by the Chair with regard to the point of order.

Basically, the situation is that for several decades farmers engaged in the volatile grain growing business in the west wanted stability of price and income. This particular bill was supposed to be the Liberal government's answer in stabilizing their income, yet we hear this type of argument that there is no difference between five minus three equals two, and four minus two equals two.
My question to the government is very simple. We are going to support this amendment because we would like to see as many farmers as possible come into this type of legislation to try to stabilize incomes. We do not think this type of legislation will bring in many farmers, but because we know the need for the stabilization of income we would like to see as many farmers as possible come in, no matter how poor the legislation.
I would like to ask the government why it is trying to stop farmers from wanting to join this program? A farmer certainly considers the costs listed in motion No. 5, the question of interest, depreciation, and the other things listed, in addition to what is in clause 8, as legitimate costs. It is easy to get these costs because we have the most efficient collector of costs in the world in the income tax branch of the Department of National Revenue.
Therefore when I hear government members stand up and say we should not accept this amendment on the ground that it is only the difference between five minus three equals two and four minus two equals two, and what you add on here you take off there, and the type of argument made by one member of our party who said it was making it more complicated than the original bill, I cannot see what the government is trying to do. Is it trying to keep farmers out of this?
I do not know who is responsible for the point of order on acceptability raised by the Chair, but if any person read the legislation, even without understanding all the complicated computerized formulas you have to understand thoroughly, it would be obvious and clear that the government's contribution was set by statute in this bill and that the farmers' contribution was set by statute in this bill. There could not be any extra charge on the government, yet we have this point of order that was raised being supported by members of the government.
Here I am, as one member of this parliament, trying to get some form of legislation on the books that gives some chance for continuous stability of income for the farmer, yet I see the actions of the government and of the members of the government party in every way that they know, trying to discourage farmers from getting into this particular type of program.
If the minister had listened to the representations we made on second reading, namely, that the bill should not be put into the standing committee but taken to the farmers to get their view before we voted on the principle, we would not be in the mess we are in today. When the minister insisted with his usual rigidity and inflexibility that we first vote on the principle and then ask the farmers, we knew that he would not change.
As I shall be pointing out, as will others on third reading, farmers do not like this type of legislation and have said so. However, we are being forced to go through this routine

we are in now of trying to amend that legislation. We are supporting this motion by the NDP on the grounds that it will add to the weight of the arguments of the government when presenting this poor bill so that more farmers will join in the program. I cannot understand why the government is opposing it at this particular time.
In conclusion I wish to suggest to the House leader that, as far as the official opposition is concerned, we would be glad to have a vote on this right away so that we can get on with it. subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION-SUGGESTION CORPORATION NOT SELECT LAWYERS FOR MORTGAGORS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION-SUGGESTION CORPORATION NOT SELECT LAWYERS FOR MORTGAGORS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my point in rising at this hour is to make the best attempt that I can to divorce an ancient and honourable provision of the law from a disgusting form of the political pork barrel.
I raised the question the other day with the Minister of State, that urbane gentleman for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson), and his reply was indistinguishable from the replies given by ministers holding his position or reporting to the House for the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation ever since CMHC was formed.
The point is simple, Mr. Speaker. If you wish, or anybody else wishes to go to CMHC to use its mortgage facilities to help buy a house, you will find that the lawyer is selected for you by CMHC or that your choice is limited to a list of lawyers presented to you by the corporation. I am not enveighing against all political patronage in the political field. I think lawyers are a large and necessary part of the forces by which any one of us is elected, and most of us realize that there is a political reality-that other things being equal you go to your friends, not to your foes. So if, for example, the Department of Fisheries needs a lawyer to prosecute a case, the present stripe of the government being Liberal I would expect that the stripe of the lawyer prosecuting for the department would be Liberal. I have no quarrel with that, because government is the client and the lawyer is the choice of that client. But I would object, and I think Canadians, if they knew the practice, should object to the government choosing our lawyers when we go to get a CMHC mortgage.
I called it a disgusting form of political patronage when I asked the minister that question and received a ho-hum answer from him, though reading his heart rather than the words he put on paper I got the impression he agrees 100 per cent with me that it is a most unenviable job he has, trying to defend the practice of government appointments, Liberal government appointments in this case, though a few years ago it was Conservative appointments; I know how these things work so I can tell Your Honour exactly what happens. I say it is morally wrong, that it should not be defended by anybody and that it should be changed.
29956-SI

November 27, 1975
Adjournment Debate	[DOT]
I say again that if government appoints lawyers for its own purposes, that is one thing. But if it appoints CMHC-approved lawyers-and they will be Liberal lawyers throughout the length and breadth of Canada-and somebody goes in and says, "I have my own lawyer who does all my work for me," then CMHC will say, "No, you have to use one of these lawyers." This, to my mind, may hurt the lawyer the client proposes, because the client might perhaps say to himself, "My lawyer is not recognized somehow by the government." That is bad. It is demeaning to the profession and I do not know why the bar associations have not hollered more about it.
I do not know why more lawyers who are members of parliament are not screaming about this dirty, filthy practice. In any event I am bringing it out, and I intend to continue doing so. I will say this, in case we get some facetious, half-baked reply to the effect that the government has to be sure of the quality of the lawyers concerned-I know the lawyers chosen by the government are good ones. The people who draw up a political patronage list of lawyers make sure of that, as far as possible, because they do not wish to approve lawyers who are likely to get them into difficulties. I know they may be good lawyers, but they are not the lawyers of my choice when I go to CMHC. The private lending institutions now generally allow you to use your own lawyer.
In closing, I point out that there is a policy of insurance in most, if not all, provinces for members of the bar. If you are stuck with a bad lemon, as once in a while you will be, some protection is given either by the bar itself or its insurance. So there is no reason whatever why this ancient, very unhappy and dirty practice that has been carried on for many decades should exist any longer in this decade. I hope that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Gauthier) will have the guts and gumption to stand up, acknowledge it is wrong, and to say that "we are putting an end to it now, go to CMHC and take along your own lawyer to do your business with that Crown corporation".

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Robert Gauthier (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION-SUGGESTION CORPORATION NOT SELECT LAWYERS FOR MORTGAGORS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been going over material dating as far back as June 18, 1959, to try to find some solution to the problem raised by the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave). I should like to quote from a letter signed by the executive secretary to the then minister of justice, Mr. Fulton:
The policy of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and indeed, of all government departments, is that no lawyer may act both for his client and the C.M.H.C. or the department at the same time. I am sure you will readily understand the reason for this rule when you consider the conflicts of interest that could arise.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford), in accordance with the responsibilities imposed upon him by his position, recommends from time to time names of legal agents across Canada who are best able to perform legal work for the Government of Canada or certain of its agencies as may be required from time to time. The present practice with respect to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is that, with the approval of the Minister of Justice, the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) from time to time provides Central Mortgage and Housing Cor-

poration with the names of legal agents who might be employed by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in various municipalities throughout Canada.
I appreciate the hon. member's point of view regarding choice of lawyer for both client and CMHC and I will bring it to the attention of my minister, who I am sure will be able to reply in much better terms than I.

AIR CANADA-LACK OF SUPPORT FOR FIVE EMPLOYEES CHARGED WITH CRIMINAL OFFENCE-BONDING OF EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
make matters worse their chances of finding part-time jobs to try to make ends meet were minimal. As one employee said in an interview in the Toronto Sun, "I couldn't even get a job to work part-time at a service station because I was facing charges-I had to borrow to live". Another contributing factor to the employee's dilemma is that the judicial system is a slow moving machine. If any appeals are to be made the process can drag on for months, with legal fees soaring and the employee not receiving any kind of moral or financial support from his employer, Air Canada.
I am not recounting a few isolated incidents. During question period I have repeatedly brought up the problems of morale in the finance department of Air Canada in Winnipeg. Last April, Air Canada employees went on strike at the Charles de Gaulle Airport in Paris. What we have here is a breakdown of employer-employee communication.
I think it is time that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) should recognize the seriousness of this problem and try to rectify the matter. I would suggest that the minister sit down with Air Canada and union officials and discuss the immediate improvement of security at all Air Canada terminals in the world. Such a move would take away some of the onus placed on Air Canada's employees when dealing with the shipment and storage of valuables. I would suggest that some sort of insurance or bonding be made available to those employees who may find themselves in the same situation as those charged with gold theft in New York. It would be to the benefit of Air Canada management to make it possible for its employees to air their views and subsequently make Air Canada a more receptive employer.
There have also been a number of robberies. On January 27, 1975, it is reported that gold and silver bars worth more than $88,000 were stolen from mailbags at Toronto International Airport. The report also stated that police said post office investigators told them on the previous Friday that $15,877 worth of gold and silver bars were stolen from the mail January 14. The report further stated that police said investigations also revealed that some time since November 14, 1974, a $72,130 gold bar weighing 399 ounces was stolen from the mail. So, Mr. Speaker, you can see that these gold thefts at Air Canada terminals represent a very serious problem. I suggest the minister should launch an immediate investigation into the whole procedure in respect of security of such valuables at airports.
Mr. fcalph E. Goodale (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport): Mr. Speaker, following the questions put to the minister in the House by the hon. member on November 24 the Ministry of Transport has made an inquiry of Air Canada to determine the circumstances surrounding the particular situation to which the hon. member has referred at Kennedy International Airport in New York. We have received the assurance from Air Canada that the security arrangement at the Kennedy International Airport, and indeed at all other airports, continues to be entirely satisfactory and that Air Canada has no apparent reason to make alterations to a system which is and has been working effectively.
I must say that the comment raised by my hon. friend in respect of a theft at the Ottawa airport a year or so ago, or
Adjournment Debate
at least in 1974, is a particular situation I should like to check into further. However, the item of concern this evening especially relates to the situation at Kennedy International Airport.
With respect to the employees who were recently acquitted of a charge of theft on the ramp at Kennedy International airport, they were all reinstated to their former positions and paid in full for the time during which they were under suspension while awaiting a hearing of their case. As the hon. member will understand, these employees were charged under normal legal procedures by the New York port authority police. They obtained legal council, and in due course were acquitted. In no way can Air Canada be held responsible for payment of their legal fees. This was, and is, in all ordinary practice a private concern of each individual employee.
On the final point raised by the hon. member in his supplementary question to the minister on the same day, November 24, with respect to the matter of bonding, Air Canada is satisfied that all its employees are properly bonded under a blanket fidelity bond which insures Air Canada against the dishonest or fraudulent act of any employee acting alone or in collusion with others.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION-SUGGESTED STUDY OF STRUCTURE AND EXPENDITURES TO PROMOTE EFFICIENCY AND REDUCE EXPENDITURES
GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION-SUGGESTED STUDY OF STRUCTURE AND EXPENDITURES TO PROMOTE EFFICIENCY AND REDUCE EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 31 I asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) to consider a Glassco Commission type study of government organization, and he responded that he thought it was a constructive suggestion which he would take up with his colleagues, so tonight I have a few suggestions in support of my proposition for the consideration of the minister.
Any administrative organization needs to be examined periodically to see how it is working compared with how it is intended to work; to test the suitability of the organization adapted to changed circumstances because any organization, instead of adapting in time, tends to lag behind changing needs; and to force those involved to examine their role and test their suitability, and be self-conscious about how it really works.	[DOT]
In the case of the federal government it is now 15 years since the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker) set up the Royal Commission on Government Organization, which was called the Glassco Commission, and 13 years since that commission made its first major report. That means, I think it is safe to say, that we are probably three to five years overdue in having another look at the whole system and how it is working. Also in that time the size and the complexity of the federal public service have both multiplied, and a tremendous amount of delegated authority has been given to public servants and extended in variety and scope.
We know that at this time there is much evidence that the government proceeds like a whole series of separate empires. These empires often compete with each other. Sometimes they even conflict with each other.
These are all reasons why it is timely to consider a new look through a new appropriately guided royal commis-
299S6-5PA

November 27, 1975
Adjournment Debate
sion. What are some of the things at which we could look? I suggest the following: first, we could look at the cost of particular operations in relation to the cost of similar functions in the private sector.
Second, we could look at new approaches to accountability. The Glassco Commission tried to establish some in both the financial and personnel management fields, but the ways in which these have been adopted certainly are not working perfectly, and the demands are greater today.
Third, we should look at some important aspects of personnel function. There is a good deal of evidence that labour relations in the public service are bad.
Fourth, we need to identify obsolete and outdated functions. Unless we look at something like the government every so often, things go on for ever even if the need for them disappears.
Fifth, we need to identify functions which could be done as well or better in the private sector. The Glassco Commission tried to identify some of these, but not very much action resulted. It is worth another try.
Sixth, we need to look at the whole organization from the standpoint of the function it is supposed to perform and its performance in fact.
With so much change in growth in the public service, and so much change in the role of government and the character of the world around the government-the external environment-there are bound to be inadequacies and things which deserve another look so that we can feel our taxes are well spent.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lloyd Francis (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION-SUGGESTED STUDY OF STRUCTURE AND EXPENDITURES TO PROMOTE EFFICIENCY AND REDUCE EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member who just spoke did make his suggestion on October 31 of this year to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald). The minister at that time indicated that the
suggestion was a constructive one which he would investigate and discuss with his colleagues.
At the present time extensive reviews are being undertaken by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) of all aspects of government operations with the objective of eliminating expenses which can be eliminated or reduced. The utmost economy is being exercised, and no doubt hon. members in this House will hear a good deal more of the consequences of that review.
The Auditor General, Mr. J. J. Macdonnell, with the full co-operation of the government, has undertaken several studies, including the report of the Independent Review Committee on the Office of the Auditor General of Canada, which was tabled in the House on April 14 of this year. In addition, the Auditor General has undertaken an extensive study in the general area of financial management and control. The government will take this opportunity to make these necessary changes in its over-all structure so as to rectify any weakness in the system which these studies may reveal.
The nature and scope of the study undertaken by the so-called Glassco commission was much broader and more extensive, and covered a substantial period of time. The government is continuing to take these matters under investigation and will undertake measures to lead to short term economies. It is reviewing the entire operation of the Auditor General, and at the end of this the government will take stock and note what further measures are required.
